title: Old Testament Literature, Torah & Biblical Covenants
description: Comprehensive certification examination testing the Pentateuch (Torah), Abrahamic & Mosaic Covenants, Tabernacle typology, Wisdom Literature, and Major Prophets.
instructions: This exam evaluates deep textual, historical, and theological understanding of the Old Testament scriptures.
AI Proctoring is enabled: Web camera, microphone monitoring, and fullscreen lock are active.
Exiting fullscreen or switching browser tabs more than 3 times will trigger automatic exam submission.
You may use the built-in Scripture Reference Sheet and Scratchpad from the toolbar.
Show clear scriptural references and theological precision in your short-answer explanations.

questions.text: In the Abrahamic Covenant (Genesis 12, 15, and 17), which dramatic ceremony in Genesis 15 signified God’s unconditional commitment to fulfill His covenant promises to Abram?

options.text: Abram built an altar on Mount Moriah and offered a ram in place of his son.
A smoking firepot and a blazing torch representing God passed between the severed animal halves while Abram slept.
Melchizedek poured oil over Abram and anointed him king of Salem.
Moses sprinkled the blood of the covenant onto the twelve stone pillars at Mount Sinai.

questions.explanation: In ancient Near Eastern covenant ceremonies, parties walked between cut animal halves pledging "May it be done to me as to these animals if I break covenant." In Genesis 15:17, only God (symbolized by the smoking firepot and blazing torch) passed between the pieces, making the covenant unilateral and unconditionally guaranteed by Yahweh.

questions.text: Explain the theological significance of the Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) ritual in Leviticus 16, specifically contrasting the roles of the two goats (the slaughtered goat and the scapegoat / Azazel), and how this prefigures biblical atonement.
questions.correctAnswer: On Yom Kippur, the high priest cast lots over two goats: 1) The first goat was slaughtered as a sin offering; its blood was brought inside the veil into the Holy of Holies and sprinkled on the Mercy Seat to make propitiation (expiation) for the people’s sins before God’s presence. 2) Over the second live goat (the scapegoat / Azazel), the priest laid hands and confessed all the iniquities of Israel, and it was sent away into the wilderness bearing their sins far away. Together they depict two complementary dimensions of atonement: propitiation (satisfaction of divine justice through blood) and expiation / remission (the removal and carrying away of sin).
questions.evaluationRubric: Candidate must explain: 1) First goat slaughtered for blood sprinkled on the Mercy Seat (propitiation / cleansing sanctuary), 2) Second live goat (scapegoat / Azazel) bearing confessed sins into the wilderness (removal of sins), and 3) Theological duality of satisfaction and removal of sin.
questions.explanation: Leviticus 16 provides the central Old Testament picture of double atonement: blood payment before God and total removal of guilt far away from the community (Psalm 103:12: "As far as the east is from the west...").

questions.text: According to Exodus 25-26 and Hebrews 9, which of the following sacred objects were placed inside the Holy of Holies (the Most Holy Place) behind the veil in the Tabernacle? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The Ark of the Covenant (containing the Tablets of the Testimony)
The Mercy Seat (Kaporet / Atonement Cover) with cherubim
The Golden Lampstand (Menorah)
The Table of Showbread

questions.explanation: The Holy of Holies contained only the Ark of the Covenant surmounted by the Mercy Seat with the golden cherubim. The Golden Lampstand and Table of Showbread were situated outside the inner veil in the Holy Place.

questions.text: True or False: When the prophet Elijah fled to Mount Horeb in fear of Jezebel (1 Kings 19), the LORD revealed His presence not in the tearing hurricane wind, the violent earthquake, or the blazing fire, but in a "gentle whisper" (still, small voice).

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. 1 Kings 19:11-12 records that the LORD was not in the wind, earthquake, or fire, but manifested in the "sound of a low whisper" (qol d’mamah daqqah), teaching Elijah that God works through quiet, persistent sovereign power.

questions.text: Contrast the strict Retribution Theology argued by Job’s friends (Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar) with the resolution revealed when God answers Job out of the whirlwind in Job 38-41.
questions.correctAnswer: Job’s three friends maintained a rigid mechanical Retribution Theology (Deuteronomic formula): righteous living always yields immediate prosperity, while suffering is definitive proof of hidden, unconfessed sin. They concluded Job must be wicked. When God answers from the whirlwind (Job 38-41), He does not charge Job with wicked deeds, nor does He explain the cosmic wager of chapters 1-2. Instead, God takes Job on a tour of the cosmos, highlighting divine sovereignty, wisdom, and the limits of human knowledge. God shows that suffering is not always punitive retribution; God’s moral order is grounded in transcendent wisdom that finite humans cannot exhaustively master.
questions.evaluationRubric: Candidate must clearly describe: 1) Friends’ Retribution Theology (suffering = direct punishment for personal sin), 2) Job’s innocence vs friends’ accusations, 3) God’s answer from the whirlwind revealing divine sovereign wisdom, majesty, and the inadequacy of human mechanical moral formulas.
questions.explanation: The Book of Job dismantles the simplistic idea that all suffering is direct punishment for personal sins, pointing instead to trust in Yahweh’s transcendent wisdom and cosmic sovereignty.

questions.text: In the Fourth Servant Song of Isaiah (Isaiah 52:13 - 53:12), which famous declaration describes the substitutionary nature of the Servant’s suffering?

options.text: "He was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace."
"Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem."
"For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government shall be upon his shoulder."
"The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat."

questions.explanation: Isaiah 53:5 is the preeminent Old Testament prophecy of vicarious substitutionary atonement, fulfilled in Jesus Christ: "He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed."

title: New Testament Gospels, Pauline Epistles & Early Church
description: Advanced assessment covering the Synoptic Gospels, Johannine Logos Christology, the Book of Acts, Pauline Soteriology (Romans & Galatians), and the Resurrection.
instructions: Proctored examination assessing critical understanding of New Testament Greek terms, theology, and historical context.
Active gaze tracking, face presence verification, and audio frequency monitoring are active.
Ensure clear scriptural citations and theological depth in all responses.

questions.text: In the Gospel of Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:17), how does Jesus define His relationship to the Law of Moses and the Prophets?

options.text: He came to abolish and repeal the Law so that commandments would no longer apply.
He came not to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill (plērosai) them.
He endorsed the oral traditions and fence-laws added by the Pharisees as equal to Scripture.
He instructed that the ceremonial dietary laws be extended worldwide without modification.

questions.explanation: In Matthew 5:17, Jesus explicitly declares: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them." He fulfills the Law’s moral demands, prophecies, and sacrificial typology.

questions.text: In Romans 3:21-26 and Galatians 2:15-21, expound the Apostle Paul’s doctrine of "Justification by Faith" (dikaiosynē theou). How does Paul argue that justification is achieved through faith in Christ apart from the works of the Law (ergōn nomou)?
questions.correctAnswer: Paul argues that all human beings, both Jews and Gentiles, have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Rom 3:23), making it impossible for anyone to be declared righteous through adherence to the works of the Law (ergōn nomou). Justification (dikaiōsis) is a judicial declaration where God declares a sinner righteous. This righteousness is not earned by moral achievement, but is received as a free gift of divine grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation (hilastērion) by His blood, received through faith. Christ took the curse of the Law (Gal 3:13), so that believers are justified by faith in Him, not by ceremonial or moral Torah-keeping.
questions.evaluationRubric: Candidate must explain: 1) Universal sinfulness of humanity (Romans 3:23), 2) Impossibility of justification by works of the Law (ergon nomou), 3) Justification as a gracious divine declaration based on Christ’s propitiatory sacrifice (hilasterion), 4) Faith as the instrument through which this righteousness is appropriated.
questions.explanation: Justification by faith alone (sola fide) through grace alone (sola gratia) in Christ alone is the cornerstone of Pauline theology. Righteousness is imputed to the believer through faith in Jesus who satisfied the Law’s demands.

questions.text: Which of the following famous "I AM" (Egō Eimi) statements with absolute predicates are spoken by Jesus exclusively in the Gospel of John? (Select all that apply)

options.text: "I am the Bread of Life" (John 6:35)
"I am the Good Shepherd" (John 10:11)
"I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life" (John 14:6)
"I am the True Vine, and my Father is the vinedresser" (John 15:1)

questions.explanation: All four statements are among the 7 distinct "I AM" sayings with predicates found exclusively in the Gospel of John, echoing the divine name revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14 ("I AM WHO I AM").

questions.text: True or False: At the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15, James and the apostles ruled that Gentile converts were required to be circumcised and observe the entirety of the Mosaic ceremonial code in order to be saved.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. The Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 concluded that Gentile believers are saved by grace through faith just as Jewish believers are, without the yoke of circumcision. They were only asked to abstain from food polluted by idols, sexual immorality, meat of strangled animals, and blood.

questions.text: Examine the Christological Carmen Christi (Hymn of Christ) in Philippians 2:5-11. Detail the stages of the *Kenosis* (Christ’s voluntary self-emptying) and His subsequent sovereign exaltation by God the Father.
questions.correctAnswer: Philippians 2:5-11 presents a profound two-movement theological arc: 1) The Descent / Kenosis: Christ, although existing in the very form of God (morphē theou), did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped (harpagmon), but emptied Himself (ekenōsen), taking the form of a servant (morphē doulou), being born in human likeness. In humility, He became obedient unto death—even death on a cross. 2) The Ascent / Divine Exaltation: Therefore, God has highly exalted Him (hyperypsōsen) and bestowed on Him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Kyrios), to the glory of God the Father.
questions.evaluationRubric: Must articulate: 1) Pre-existence in the form of God (morphe theou), 2) Self-emptying (kenosis) taking servant form and human likeness, 3) Obedience to death on a cross, and 4) Super-exaltation by God with universal confession as Lord (Kyrios).
questions.explanation: Philippians 2:5-11 is one of the earliest and most elevated Christological passages in the New Testament, grounding Christian humility and ethics in the incarnation, cross, and cosmic lordship of Jesus.

title: Biblical Hermeneutics, Theology & Scriptural Doctrines
description: Assessment evaluating principles of grammatical-historical exegesis, the doctrine of Scripture, biblical typology, and the unity of the Triune Godhead.
instructions: Standard biblical interpretation and doctrine examination.
You are provided with an on-screen Scripture reference guide and formula sheet.
Adhere strictly to grammatical-historical interpretative principles.

questions.text: In biblical interpretation, what is the crucial distinction between *exegesis* and *eisegesis*?

options.text: Exegesis interprets poetry literally, while eisegesis allegorizes historical narratives.
Exegesis draws out the author’s intended meaning from the text, while eisegesis reads the reader’s preconceived ideas into the text.
Exegesis applies strictly to the Old Testament, while eisegesis is used for the New Testament.
Exegesis translates texts word-for-word, while eisegesis paraphrases dynamic equivalents.

questions.explanation: Exegesis (from Greek "to lead out") means objectively drawing out what the biblical author originally meant in historical, grammatical, and literary context. Eisegesis (from Greek "to lead in") is the error of imposing one’s own presuppositions and biases into the biblical text.

questions.text: Explain the biblical doctrine of the Trinity, demonstrating from Scripture both the essential unity of God (Monotheism) and the eternal distinction and full deity of the three Persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit).
questions.correctAnswer: The doctrine of the Trinity teaches that there is only one true and living God (Deuteronomy 6:4 Shema: "The LORD our God, the LORD is one"; Isaiah 45:5), existing eternally as three distinct, co-equal, co-eternal Persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. 1) The Father is fully God (1 Cor 8:6). 2) The Son is fully God (John 1:1 "the Word was God"; Colossians 2:9 "in Him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily"; Hebrews 1:8). 3) The Holy Spirit is fully God and a personal being (Acts 5:3-4 where lying to the Spirit is lying to God; 1 Cor 2:10-11). The three Persons are distinct yet undivided in essence, seen united at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:16-17), the Great Commission baptismal formula (Matthew 28:19: singular "name" of Father, Son, Spirit), and the Apostolic blessing (2 Cor 13:14).
questions.evaluationRubric: Candidate must include: 1) Biblical Monotheism (one essence / Deuteronomy 6:4), 2) Full deity of the Father, Son (John 1:1/Col 2:9), and Spirit (Acts 5:3-4), 3) Eternal personal distinction, 4) Scriptural synthesis (Matthew 28:19, 2 Cor 13:14).
questions.explanation: Orthodox Christian theology affirms one God in three Persons (una substantia, tres personae). They share the same divine nature and attributes while relating in distinct personal ways in the economy of salvation.

questions.text: Which of the following are explicitly listed by the Apostle Paul as the "Fruit of the Spirit" in Galatians 5:22-23? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Love (Agapē), Joy, and Peace
Patience, Kindness, and Goodness
Faithfulness, Gentleness, and Self-control
Financial Prosperity and Worldly Power

questions.explanation: Galatians 5:22-23 lists 9 virtues as the single harvest fruit of the Holy Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Option D is contrary to biblical cruciform discipleship.

questions.text: True or False: The Reformation hermeneutical rule of "Scriptura Scripturae Interpres" (Scripture is its own interpreter / Analogy of Faith) means that obscure or difficult biblical passages should be interpreted in the light of clear, unambiguous passages.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. The principle of the Analogy of Faith (analogia fidei) asserts that because Scripture is divinely inspired and coherent, Scripture interprets Scripture; no individual passage should be interpreted in a way that contradicts the clear teaching of the rest of the Bible.

title: Biblical Languages: Hebrew & Koine Greek Exegesis
description: Advanced philological and exegetical certification on Old Testament Hebrew and New Testament Koine Greek grammar, vocabulary, syntax, and discourse analysis.
instructions: This exam tests advanced lexical semantics and grammatical syntax in Biblical Hebrew and Koine Greek.
AI Proctoring is actively monitoring camera feed, microphone levels, and tab changes.
Scripture and Biblical Language reference sheet is available in the toolbar.
Provide precise morphological parsing and semantic justifications in short-answer prompts.

questions.text: What is the primary theological nuance of the Hebrew noun "Hesed" (חֶסֶד), prominent throughout the Psalms and the Book of Ruth?

options.text: Fleeting sentimental compassion that depends on human merit
Steadfast, loyal covenant love and enduring faithfulness grounded in Yahweh’s character
Ritual ceremonial purity required for priests entering the holy place
Military valor and physical triumph over national adversaries

questions.explanation: Hesed (חֶסֶד) is the covenantal love and unconditional loyalty of God toward His covenant people, expressing faithfulness that perseveres through human failure (Exodus 34:6, Psalm 136).

questions.text: Analyze the Greek clause "Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος" (In the beginning was the Word) from John 1:1. Explain the theological significance of the imperfect verb "ἦν" (ēn) compared to the aorist verb "ἐγένετο" (egeneto) used in John 1:14 ("the Word became flesh").
questions.correctAnswer: In John 1:1, the verb ἦν (ēn) is in the imperfect active indicative of eimi (to be), indicating continuous, eternal existence without point of origin—the Logos already was continuously existing before creation began ("en archē"). In contrast, in John 1:14, John shifts to ἐγένετο (egeneto), the aorist indicative of ginomai (to become/come into being). The Word did not "become" God; rather, the eternally existing Word "became flesh" at a specific historical point in time in the Incarnation, taking on genuine human nature without ceasing to be the eternal Logos.
questions.evaluationRubric: Candidate must explain: 1) The imperfect "ēn" signifying eternal, continuous pre-existence of the Logos, 2) The contrast with aorist "egeneto" in John 1:14 denoting an entry into historical human existence, and 3) The theological implication for Christ’s eternal deity and temporal Incarnation.
questions.explanation: The grammatical contrast between ēn (eternal continuous being) in John 1:1 and egeneto (point-in-time historical becoming) in John 1:14 is a cornerstone of New Testament Christology.

questions.text: Which of the following theological assertions are true regarding the Hebrew verb "Bara" (בָּרָא) in Genesis 1:1? (Select all that apply)

options.text: In the Qal stem, God (Elohim) is the exclusive grammatical subject of "Bara" across the Old Testament.
It denotes the bringing into being of entirely novel reality without requiring pre-existing material.
It is synonymous with ordinary human craftsmanship like carpentry or metalworking.
It underscores God’s sovereign, effortless cosmic creation by His Word.

questions.explanation: Throughout the Hebrew Bible, bara (בָּרָא) in the Qal stem has only God as its subject, never humans, signifying divine creation ex nihilo and effortless sovereign power. Human craftsmanship uses verbs like asah or yatsar.

questions.text: True or False: In Koine Greek verbal aspect, the Aorist tense primarily communicates a "continuous, ongoing, linear" action in time.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. The Aorist tense in Greek represents "perfective" verbal aspect—viewing an action as a complete whole or snapshot ("summary" aspect), whereas the Present and Imperfect tenses convey imperfective (continuous, ongoing, linear) aspect.
